I chose to study the Los Angeles Police Department's predictive policing practices. In the 2010s, LAPD ran two such programs: one using PredPol, and one called Operation LASER.

PredPol was a place-based, proprietary predictive policing algorithm used from roughly 2011 to April 2020. While active, it predicted crime at a fine spatial grain (~500ft grid cells), recalculated per shift, and directed patrol resources to those predicted cells, or "hotspots."

PredPol faced substantial criticism during its implementation. @the-markup_2021_how-we-determined found that PredPol's predictions disproportionately targeted low-income Black and Latino neighborhoods. Part of the problem traces to what the tool was trained on: place-based predictive tools like PredPol are trained on police-recorded crime and calls-for-service, not independent crime data [@lum-isaac_2016_to-predict-and-serve]. Reported crime is partly a product of policing intensity itself: more patrolling means more discovery of low-level offenses, which leads to more recorded incidents, which causes the algorithm to flag that area again, creating a feedback loop. Victim reporting itself is not a clean baseline either: reporting rates are suppressed in over-policed and immigrant communities due to distrust of police, so no available data source (police records, calls for service, victimization surveys) offers unpolluted ground truth on true crime location at fine geography.

Place-based algorithms like PredPol also raise Fourth Amendment and equal-protection concerns rather than classic due-process ones, since in concentrated stops no individual is notified or given a chance to contest. Operation LASER's person-based "Chronic Offender" infrastructure is a closer fit for a due-process critique, and it matters here because DICFP's ACCIC and CAPRA units trace directly back to it [@stop-lapd-spying-coalition_2021_automating-banishment], meaning DICFP inherits person-based due-process exposure alongside PredPol's place-based legacy. Underlying all of this are two competing interpretations of PredPol's actual role, neither resolved by available data: algorithm-as-driver, where PredPol independently concentrated policing beyond what existing patrol patterns would have produced, versus algorithm-as-encoder, where PredPol simply encoded pre-existing patrol biases and the underlying deployment logic never really changed when the algorithm was introduced.

Ultimately, PredPol was discontinued due to budget constraints driven by the COVID-19 crisis. It was replaced by Data-Informed, Community-Focused Policing (DICFP), launched that same month (April 2020), which LAPD stated was aimed at building trust, reducing violent crime, and assisting victims [@los-angeles-police-department_2020_data-informed-community-focused].

The program was only partially transparent. Underlying crime incident and arrest data are public via data.lacity.org (LAPD Crime Incidents, LAPD Arrest data). But the algorithm's actual predicted outputs, the box-level, per-shift predictions, were never systematically public; the Markup only obtained fragments via records requests for specific divisions and periods, not a full city-wide panel. No public data links those predicted boxes to actual officer dispatch or patrol behavior, so it was impossible to verify whether officers actually complied with or acted on the algorithm's predictions. This lack of transparency can at least partially be attributed to PredPol's status as a private vendor: it had no requirement to disclose proprietary model outputs, and there was no systematic public disclosure requirement for algorithmic policing tools' internal predictions or compliance data more broadly.

Overall, this was a poor implementation of predictive policing. Even the evidence on whether it achieved its core crime-reduction goal is genuinely contested, not settled. @mohler-etal_2015_randomized-controlled-field is the strongest positive evidence: a real randomized controlled trial, including a direct arm within three LAPD divisions (Foothill, North Hollywood, and Southwest), found PredPol's ETAS algorithm modestly outperformed analyst-driven hotspot maps, producing a 7.4% reduction in crime volume as a function of patrol time. That trial has two real limitations worth naming. Some of its authors held a financial stake in PredPol Inc., a conflict of interest, and the paper does not disclose a random or representativeness-based method for selecting those three divisions out of LAPD's roughly 21. The trial dates track PredPol's actual sequential rollout (Foothill was its original 2011 pilot site), suggesting a convenience sample rather than one chosen to generalize to the department as a whole. Meanwhile, other research directly contradicts this finding: a RAND Corporation evaluation of a 2012 randomized trial in Shreveport, Louisiana found no statistically significant reduction in property crime in the districts that received predictive policing, compared to the districts that did not [@hunt-etal_2014_evaluation-shreveport-predictive]. Early pilot numbers from Atlanta (8-9% decline in treated zones), Santa Cruz (19% burglary decline over six months), and Kent (6% violent crime decline) are largely vendor- and department-reported figures from early adoption, not independently verified at RCT standards [@snider_2026_what-works-in-american-policing]. In short, the single best-designed study found a modest positive effect with real caveats, while comparably rigorous independent trials found none.

Even setting that contested evidence aside, predictive policing could modestly reduce crime and still not be worth its cost. A tool that concentrates a fixed patrol budget onto predicted hotspots can mechanically raise the arrest-to-reported-crime ratio in exactly the areas it targets, since more patrol produces more arrests without a proportional rise in reported crime, and this can happen even as citywide crime falls in aggregate. Reducing crime overall and increasing local overpolicing are not contradictory findings; they can be the same mechanism described from two different angles. Compounding this, it is impossible to cleanly attribute any change, or lack of change, after PredPol's discontinuation to the algorithm specifically. Removal is further confounded by the simultaneous George Floyd protests and national policing reckoning, on top of the COVID-19 budget crisis already noted above.

What should LAPD have done instead? If crime is significantly underreported in some areas, any tool trained on reported crime will be systematically biased, and fixing that bias requires crime data independent of policing intensity. That kind of data would need to be precise and granular, and it is not currently publicly collected. A more promising direction would be for LAPD, or independent researchers, to partner with community organizations to survey where crime is over- or under-reported, so that enforcement intensity could finally be checked against something other than the police's own contaminated data.
